content.thinking:
I'm picturing an African bush elephant rendered in low-poly style—large fan-shaped ears, swaybacked body, trunk with ridges, tusks, and a limited gray flat-color palette with faceted geometric shapes.

Now I'm working out the actual proportions and skeleton: shoulder height around 3.2m, body barrel width ~1.8m, legs tapering from thick columns to narrower ankles, head positioned higher than the withers with a curling trunk and forward-curving tusks, and I'm sketching out the bone hierarchy starting from hips through the spine chain.

Now I'm planning the neck and head geometry, with a short neck chain connecting to a large skull with a forehead dome, then sketching the trunk root hanging from the face and curving forward through six joints down to its tip.

The trunk tapers from a wider base to a thin tip, with ring-like wrinkles painted along its length and two small finger-like lobes at the end plus nostril detailing. I'm also planning a separate lower jaw with a chin beneath the trunk base, and sketching large flat ears extruded as planes.

Working out ear geometry now, shaping an Africa-like outline mirrored for left and right, attached at the sides of the head with hinge joints for a slight flap motion, and figuring out the extrusion direction and thickness vectors.

For the ear surface I'm planning pinkish-gray mottled paint with darker rims and subtle vein lines via noise, sized roughly 1.3m by 1.5m for the bush. I'm keeping it low-poly with flat shading and sharp, unsmoothed corners for the outline.

Now I'm working out the front leg rigging — pillar-like with slight bends, joints from shoulder to elbow to wrist to a flat round foot, placing hip near y=2.05 and the foot sole at y=0.

For the hind legs I'm adding a slight stifle/hock bend to keep them columnar like a real elephant's, and tapering the leg radii from wider at top to narrower at the ankle, with low-poly faceted sides and a short wide frustum foot shape with toenail details.

For the skin, I'm planning a mottled gray paint with countershading (lighter belly tone) and wrinkle/fold texture at the knees and ankles, since the brief calls for paints to carry fine surface detail rather than extra geometry.

Nested paints return other paints, defined in model space for continuity. I'm sizing the texture resolution to balance texel density for fine wrinkle detail against atlas limits, leaning toward 2048, and planning flat-colour materials separately for tusks, nails, and eyes while the tail gets its own chain setup.

Tail hangs from the rump with four thin joints ending in a dark bristle tuft. Tusks curve forward from the head via bezier paths with ivory coloring and a darker base ring, while eyes are small dark spheres with amber rings positioned at the sides of the head.

Now I'm detailing the eye area with a darker wrinkle ring and lashes, then shaping the head itself—a skull chain with the head joint angled forward-down, giving an African elephant's single high-domed, sloped forehead leading into the trunk base.

I'm building the head as a loft across several stations from the back of the skull forward to the trunk base, binding it to the head bone, and adding details like a temporal gland streak under the eye and a lower jaw wedge near the trunk base with its own jaw joint.

Now I'm routing the trunk as a hanging chain of path points starting wide near the head and curling slightly forward and upward at the tip, checking that the tip sits just above the floor with a natural S-curve shape and roughly correct real-world trunk length.

I'm assigning trunk joints the "tentacle" role among the broader joint taxonomy, then thinking about adding skin texture via painted dark rings along the trunk's surface parameter, with an option to also sculpt actual ridge geometry by modulating the sweep radius sinusoidally for realism.

Considering a faceted, ridged trunk with 8-sided sweeps and periodic radius bumps to create visible rings — balancing triangle count against the signature low-poly look, I'm leaning toward fewer, denser ridges (~14) using a triangle-wave radius function, then testing the result visually.

Now I'm moving to the body loft: setting up elephant proportions (chest width ~1.3, height ~1.9) and placing spine-aligned stations with a belly shift to get that characteristic hanging-belly silhouette.

I'm figuring out the back profile along the spine — shoulder height around 3.2, dipping slightly at mid-body, rising again at the hips, with the rump tapering down toward the tail — and working out the vertical center and half-height values at each station so the top and bottom surfaces land where I want them, including a low belly clearance so the legs reach the floor properly. I'm also sketching the spine as a smooth Catmull-Rom path through a few key control points along the body length.

Now I'm working through how the rump should extend past the hip joint, since the loft path needs an extra station beyond the hip to round out the rump rather than ending abruptly at the joint, while keeping bone influence tied to the chain joints before and after that point. I'm also reasoning about whether to add a separate hips joint at the base of the spine chain, how it would sit at essentially the same position as the first spine joint, and how that affects bone weighting during skinning.

Then I'm sketching out the neck: since the elephant's neck is short, I plan to cover it almost entirely with a short two-joint chain running from chest to head base, letting the body and head lofts overlap enough that a distinct neck shape isn't really needed.

For the head I'm thinking of placing a single joint near the front of the head angled slightly down and forward, with a low-poly loft forming the skull. I'm considering using flat faceted shading (smooth:false, 8 sides) across the sweeps to give the model a chunky, low-poly look consistent with the rest of the body.

Now I'm working out the leg attachments: shoulder and hip joints sit inside the body mass, with leg tubes starting visibly beneath it, using smooth skinning with painted creases at elbows/knees and folds at the ankles plus toenails for detail. For the hind legs, I'm placing hip joints near the back of the body and setting bend hints so the knee points forward and the hock angles back, building the limb chain with multiple segments to get a natural digitigrade bend.

I'm checking that the foot targets stay within reach of the combined leg segment lengths, then defining the joint chain (hip, knee, ankle, foot) with four named points for three spans plus a tip, finishing with a simple low-poly cylindrical shape for the foot itself.

I'll cap the leg with a cylinder and add a flared faceted collar at the ankle to suggest the elephant's skin folds, a nice touch of realism.

I'm placing toenails on the foot tip joint, four for front feet and three for hind, as small rounded light gray-tan boxes along the front lip, then setting foot bottoms near ground level with a small floor allowance before moving on to the trunk tip, eyes, tusk, tail, ear, and painted wrinkle details on the body.

I'm adding sparse hair cards too—small bristle tufts on the head crown, a tail brush, chin whiskers, and maybe trunk bristles—plus dust and mud painted onto the lower legs and belly, gradient wrinkle rings, neck and belly skin folds, and painted veins on the ears.

Now I'm layering in finer anatomical details: darkened ear rims, toenails, worn tusk tips with brownish stain near the base, a mouth line, a dark temporal gland streak below the eye, amber irises with dark pupils, eyelashes, lower lip, and ringed tail segments. I'm also notching small scars into the ear outline, adding dusty mud-splash patches on the flanks, and placing a few low-poly wrinkle ridges around the knees using rotated wedge shapes.

Now I'm thinking through how to generate skin fold ridges at the joints by sweeping thin ring loops around the leg geometry at the knee, ankle, and wrist — using loop paths derived from the surface sweep at each joint point, with a few ridges clustered near the ankle and fewer at the knee, plus shallow folds around the neck base.

I'm setting up coordinates so right is world negative X, mirroring the left/right sides with a sign factor, and planning joint orientation using a chain builder with parent/child naming. Now I'm starting to write the actual import statements for the builder, frame, and paint utility functions (mix, noise, cells, smoothstep, gradient, etc.) needed for the mesh generation script.

I'm defining a flat color palette for the creature's skin, nails, eyes, bristles, mouth, and tusk staining, then starting to set up the base grey tones for the skin shading.

Writing paint function...

I want to elongate wrinkles horizontally for the elephant look, so I'm stretching the y-coordinate before feeding it into the cells function, which makes creases ring-like around legs and crack-like on the body. The trunk gets its own paint treatment with ring creases, using a path length of roughly 2.6.

For ear painting, I'm working out the geometry: rim is darker gray, inner ear is lighter mottled pink-gray, and veins branch outward from the root point using angle-based bands with some noise wobble so they look organic rather than perfectly radial.

Reconsidering the angle, I want the ear plane closer to the sagittal plane for a more natural resting position, flared out around 20° rather than 27°, with the ear spanning roughly 1.2m back and 1.3m wide by 1.5m tall, attached along a vertical line at the root.

I'm sketching the low-poly outline for the ear as a jagged, Africa-map-like silhouette with sharp corners (no smoothing), running from the top attachment point down through a rounded outer rim to a pointed tip around 2m below, though I'm second-guessing the scale since a real bush elephant ear is closer to 1.5m wide by 1.8m tall.

I'll settle on a slightly smaller ear, roughly 1.25m wide by 1.7m tall, attaching at the side of the head near x=0.5. I'm planning the rig as a single hinge joint at the top so the ear can flap, with a thin rigid extrusion (~0.04 thick) for the body and a second, slightly thicker extrusion along the same outline to form a folded rim ridge.

Now I'm working out the ear's joint placement and orientation, positioning it near the top of the head aimed back and outward, then moving on to defining the head's loft shape with stations along the z-axis specifying width and height from the back of the skull up toward the crown, checking that the top height stays proportional to the withers.

Continuing, I'm shaping the lower head and cheek bulges through the loft stations down to the face front, deciding where the trunk root emerges from the face with a small circular cross-section and an initial downward path, then starting to think through the jaw placement.

I'm positioning the lower jaw as a small frustum box beneath the trunk base, sized to taper slightly and sit under the head's bottom loft point near the front, giving the chin a visible but modest presence relative to the trunk hanging in front of it.

Now I'm working out the tusks, which sprout from the upper jaw on either side of the trunk base and curve outward, downward, then forward and up -- I'm sketching a bezier sweep path with control points to get that curling shape.

I'm making sure the tusks' width stays clear of the trunk, adding a darker gum-colored ring near the tusk base to suggest the lip sheath, then moving on to placing the eyes on the head.

Now I'm working out the eye placement using surface coordinates relative to the head center, planning small sphere geometries for the eyeball and pupil, plus a subtle flattened sphere above for brow wrinkles and an eyelid ring.

For lashes I'm generating a ring of small spikes around the eye hit point, angled outward with dark coloring, then considering a thin dark streak running from the eye down for the temporal gland.

For the body, I'm adding bumpy sphere protrusions at the hip sides and shoulder blades to suggest visible bone structure under the skin, each painted as part of the skin texture. I'll let the belly sag naturally and skip genitals for simplicity.

For the tail, I'm sprouting it from the rump with a curved path down through four joints, tapering the radius from 0.07 to 0.03 near the tip, and finishing with a bristly dark tuft made of spike rings and small cards around the last joint.

Now I'm adding sparse dark bristle cards on the crown of the head, and thinking through the trunk tip — extending a small finger-like capsule forward with a lower lip, a flattened end plane, and a dark pink or oval nostril disc to give it that distinctive elephant-trunk-tip look from the front.

I'm plotting the trunk's curling path point by point, sketching the segment lengths and tangent directions so the tip curves forward and down naturally with the nostril faces oriented correctly.

At the tip I'm placing two dark nostril discs angled along the final tangent, plus a small skin-colored spike on top to act as the "finger" feature, keeping the geometry simple rather than building a full lathe shape.

For the trunk rings, I'm computing the radius as a tapering function from .30 down to .09, modulated by a triangle wave to create ridge-like creases along its length, using 8-sided smooth rings — roughly 60 rings for about 1000 triangles, which should stay performant. For shading, I'm darkening the underside and the groove creases between rings to sell the wrinkled skin look.

I'm making the ring paint function fall back to the shared body skin paint when not in a groove, and a darker grey when it is, giving a hard low-poly edge rather than blending, which should be fine visually. Now I'm defining the spine and hip joint positions for the body loft, starting from the hips and working up through a path of spine coordinates.

I'm then setting up the neck chain joints connecting the spine to the head joint, and sketching out the loft stations from rump to chest with their y position, width, and height at each z depth, starting near the tail root.

Checking the rump station placement against the hip joint, then thinking through body width versus leg spacing—legs should sit just inside the body outline near the top for a natural elephant proportion.

Settling on a body width of 1.6, I'm positioning shoulders and hips with joint coordinates, checking foot target distance against total leg reach to confirm the bends work out. I'm tapering leg radii from thick at the top to narrower near the foot, planning the leg as a smooth tube with the hip portion tucked inside the body.

For the feet, I'm sizing a tapered cylinder for the foot disc at each leg's base, positioning it so the bottom sits near ground level with a slight bevel on top. I'm also adding small flat boxes as toe nails arranged in an arc around the front of each foot, with four nails for the fore feet and three for the hind feet.

Still working out nail geometry and rotation...

I'm skipping the tilt and using a simple y-rotation to orient each nail outward, aligning it with the angle around the toe. For the ankle, I'm planning skin fold ridges as small swept loops at a few points along the leg tube.

I'm now setting the hip and front leg joint positions along the z-axis, and foot targets to match, then applying a shared skin-colored paint consistently across the body, head, neck, legs, ears, trunk, tail, and shoulder bumps so everything reads as one continuous surface. For scapula and hip bone bumps, I'm placing small sphere details directly on the body surface using angular coordinates around a reference point.

I'm working out the azimuth and elevation angles for hip and shoulder bone bumps, then adding a subtle spine ridge running along the top of the body using a sweep with tapering radius and a slight lift, sliced to cover most of the back length.

I'm also thinking through chest and neck wrinkle loops wrapped around the body surface, deciding to skip the mouth line for now and focus on trunk base folds and forehead ridge details. For the ear, I'm setting up the attachment joint at the head with a hinge direction so it can pivot naturally from its base point.

Checking the ear's position so it doesn't overlap awkwardly with the shoulder, calculating its x/z offsets relative to the body's half-width so it sits correctly behind the head.

Adjusting ear height so the tip reaches a more realistic shoulder/elbow level, revising the outline coordinates to scale it down.

Still refining the ear shape... For the ear painting, I'm working out rim shading versus interior coloring with pinkish veining, using angle-based noise around the root and surface normals to distinguish rim areas from face regions for lighter edge banding.

For base colors I'll use grayish-brown tones like African elephant skin. Then for texture cards I'm sketching hair strand SVGs with curved dark strokes, tufts of three strands, tail brush spikes, and scattered crown hair cards placed on the upper head region with controlled spacing and leaning angles.

I'll skip whiskers and extra trunk bristle detail to keep things manageable, but I'll add a sparse scatter of small hair cards along the spine and neck for a modest back-hair effect. Now I'm moving into code structure, starting with the skeleton setup and figuring out how limb joints connect — defining a limb function that takes root, target, lengths, and bends, with leg roots parented to the nearest spine joint for the hip connections.

Now I'm working out the bend directions for front and hind legs to get the elbow and knee angles pointing the right way, checking that the limb lengths give enough reach between the joints.

I'm also planning the leg sweep mesh generation and adding subtle belly shading for the underside before writing the full quadruped code.

For the legs, I'm using the chain's point array as a polyline path with named joints for the knee and foot, letting the smooth skin round the corners naturally rather than switching to a catmull spline. The foot bone will reference the tip joint of the leg chain.

For ridge loops, I'm using the chain point at a given t as the loop center, since its facing axis naturally points perpendicular to the leg—exactly the direction I need for the loop orientation. I'm also settling on colors: a muted mauve for the gum/mouth, amber eyes with near-black pupils, and I'm about to work out a striped paint pattern for the tusks.

For the tusks I want a gradient from gum color near the base to ivory further out, blended with grain-like noise texture and some brownish staining near the base fading to a lighter, worn tip. I'm thinking through how to combine smoothstep blending with noise-based grain lines in the paint function, then moving on to writing it and checking triangle counts via the snap report.

Now I'm sketching the body: skipping the spine ridge for now, leaving the neck smooth, and treating the head as a rounded loft without a separate forehead bump. For the lower jaw I'm using a frustum box with a jaw joint anchored near the head, adding chin bristle cards, and considering a small dark wedge or slab to suggest the mouth cavity between the jaw and head.

I still need to verify the mouth cavity placement visually once rendered, and I'm setting up a safe surface-hit helper that guards against null results. For the eyes, I'm looping over left/right sides, finding surface hit points on the skull, and sticking small wrinkled eye-socket spheres there, though I'm unsure about the exact type for the scale option in the stick function and will need to check it against the type definitions before finalizing.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/africanElephantSonnet/ && grep -n "StickOptions\|PartOptions" -B2 -A22 src/parts.ts | head -120; grep -n "flat" src/*.ts | head -20
